title: Choose the question, then map the body study: CT, MRI and ultrasound in cancer imaging
description: Original teaching on modality-to-question matching, protocol comparability, body-compartment mapping and uncertainty-calibrated reporting; uses the public institutional fellowship description only for its explicit rotation examples.
educationalLimits: No patient-specific imaging order, contrast administration advice, diagnosis, staging assignment, or treatment recommendation. Local protocol and clinician review govern practice.
coverageGaps: Disease-site TNM systems, organ-specific contrast protocols, and detailed treatment-related imaging findings require current site-specific guidance and supervised practice.
sourceLimitations: Automated source-fidelity review compares the exact rendered script and labels only to retrieved supporting excerpts; it is not whole-book clinical validation and does not replace qualified human clinical validation.

sections.title: Translate the question into coverage and contrast
sections.narration: A useful protocol discussion begins with a sentence, not a scanner menu: “What decision is this examination meant to inform?” In this chapter we will not prescribe a patient-specific protocol. We will learn how to state the question, identify the coverage and technical limits needed to answer it, and document what is not known. Dana-Farber's Cancer Imaging Program description gives a concrete adult body-imaging map. Its thoracic and abdominal CT experiences focus on interpreting and protocoling initial cancer staging and oncologic follow-up. The MRI curriculum names advanced cancer-related abdomen and pelvis applications, including prostate, rectal, hepatobiliary, female pelvic and MR urography examinations. Ultrasound assignments include abdominal, male and female pelvic/genitourinary, thyroid, basic vascular and superficial soft-tissue examinations. Those examples show the training's modality scope; they do not constitute a universal protocol manual. The same page says MRI and CT teaching occurs across named subspecialties and multiple modalities, which is an institutional programme fact rather than a claim of clinical comparative accuracy. [1] The ACR Appropriateness Criteria are described by ACR as evidence-based guidelines to assist referring providers in making appropriate imaging or treatment decisions. Treat this as a scenario-specific reference, not a substitute for the clinical question, local protocol, or supervising clinician. The ACR Manual on Contrast Media is a separate reference. Its public page points to the full manual and describes updated chapters and reaction cards. It supports checking a current authoritative resource when a contrast question arises. It does not let an independent learner create a screening algorithm or direct the administration of contrast. [2] [3] We can organize a hypothetical staging request into five fields: disease question; anatomy that must be covered; modality and contrast assumptions; relevant comparison; and factors that might make the study nondiagnostic or incomparable. The point is not to choose a specific contrast phase from a generic rule. It is to notice when the request, acquisition and conclusion do not line up. If a referral asks about pelvic anatomy but only a limited upper-abdominal examination is provided, the report cannot claim a complete pelvic assessment. If a follow-up examination uses a different field of view, sequence or reconstruction, a change may be real, technical, or both; the report should say whether the comparison can support the desired conclusion. The technique is a reasoning scaffold, not a clinical order. [1] [3] A fictional example: a team requests “reassess pelvic disease” but the report has no pathology subtype, previous imaging date, or treatment interval. A learner should not solve this by announcing that MRI is always preferable or that CT is insufficient. Instead, ask what local anatomy and decision are at issue; determine what the previous study can compare; confirm the acquisition includes the needed field; and request missing context. The DFCI page identifies pelvic MRI as part of the program's MRI curriculum, but does not claim every pelvic question has one prescribed modality. ACR's scenario-based criteria may inform a current modality comparison after the precise clinical scenario is clarified. The gap is meaningful: changing the wording of a request from “staging” to “response” may alter the required comparison and response framework. [1] [3]

sections.title: Use a compartment map without jumping to stage
sections.narration: For a body study, a repeatable inventory prevents a visually striking finding from erasing the rest of the examination. On a conceptual diagram, mark the primary region, local extension, regional structures, distant sites included in the field, postoperative changes and unexpected findings. This is an inventory, not a staging system. It helps the reader distinguish “not evaluated” from “evaluated and not seen,” a difference that matters whenever the examination has limited coverage. The ABR Qualifying Core blueprint confirms that GI and GU domains encompass multiple modalities and broad abnormality classes, including neoplasia and post-operative findings. This curriculum borrows those domain labels only as a board-domain map; it does not claim to teach every listed subject or to predict examination results. [4] Now consider the abdomen in a fictional patient with a newly diagnosed tumour. Before asking whether one focal abnormality changes stage, identify its organ, compartment, relation to the known primary, and whether the series can characterize it. For an indeterminate small liver finding, an oncology learner should state the image observation and identify the limitation of the current exam. A finding's proximity to a tumour does not establish its histology. The same principle applies to abdominal nodes, bowel changes, renal masses and adrenal findings: write what the image actually supports, distinguish a map from an etiologic diagnosis, and do not infer a full pathologic stage without the criteria and required clinical information. Where an ACR topic applies, consult that topic's current criteria and version with the qualified care team. [3] [4] The pelvis adds postoperative and treatment-altered anatomy. A fictional patient has a prior pelvic operation, a new MRI sequence and a follow-up CT with different coverage. First record what examination exists and what anatomy is seen. Then identify the comparator and note that a modality change may alter conspicuity. Do not interpret an apparent size difference without checking acquisition, plane and boundaries. Do not replace the oncologic question with a generic contrast-risk lecture. The ACR Manual is relevant to contrast-media reference and risk discussion, but the specific decision belongs to current local policy and qualified personnel. In the Dana-Farber public description, pelvic and GU ultrasound and advanced pelvis MRI are examples of training, not patient-specific directions. [1] [2] Worked exercise: fictional report request says “progression in abdomen” and lists a baseline scan, a follow-up scan with a smaller field, and a recent surgery. Draft a defensible interpretation plan. Model answer: (1) clarify whether the request is routine clinical assessment or a protocol-defined trial endpoint; (2) compare only the body regions captured at both timepoints; (3) inventory the primary-site region, organs, nodal stations and peritoneal/operative compartments that are actually included; (4) describe new or changing findings while flagging the reduced coverage and surgery as interpretive context; (5) avoid a global progression label until the framework and missing coverage are reconciled. This answer is defensible because each step follows from the limitations of evidence rather than from an unsupported assumption about tumour biology. [1] [3] [4]

sections.title: Contrast reference, comparability and report construction
sections.narration: A contrast question is a structured handoff, not a memory test. Record whether the question concerns iodinated or gadolinium-based agents, what the ordering team says about prior reactions or relevant history, and which institutional policy governs. The public ACR Manual page points to the full manual, lists core chapters (including topics such as metformin, pediatric use, breastfeeding, and nephrogenic systemic fibrosis), and provides downloadable reaction-treatment tables and the complete PDF. The practical habit is to use the current manual and your local response pathway, not a personal summary. A chapter page alone does not contain every individual risk decision. It is not a basis for independent prescribing or for instructing a patient to stop medication. [2] Before writing the impression, separate five ideas: clinical question, technical adequacy, observation, interpretation and next communication need. A factual observation can be certain while its cause remains uncertain. For example, a fictional follow-up study may show an unchanged small soft-tissue focus, but if the study is noncontrast and the baseline was contrast-enhanced, the ability to compare enhancement is limited. State the difference. If the local protocol directs an additional acquisition or review, that decision belongs to the responsible service. The learner's job is to communicate the evidence limitation and request the appropriate authorized decision. [1] [2] Learner exercise: Choose the strongest statement for a fictional abdominal surveillance study with incomplete lower pelvic coverage and a different MRI sequence than the baseline. A: “No disease anywhere in abdomen or pelvis.” B: “No interval disease because the visible lesion is stable.” C: “Within the imaged upper abdomen, no new finding is identified; the lower pelvis is not included and direct comparison of the sequence-dependent signal is limited.” D: “Change treatment because the MRI differs.” The correct answer is C. A overclaims coverage; B extrapolates a local observation to unseen anatomy; D converts an imaging description into treatment. C states the field, comparator limit and evidence scope. [1] [3] The take-home method is not to force certainty. It is to align the question, coverage, acquisition, comparison and conclusion. When they align, communicate the answer. When they do not, document exactly where they diverge. This makes a report more reproducible and gives the clinical team a precise information gap to resolve. This chapter supports conceptual literacy only. It is not a complete thoracic, gastrointestinal, genitourinary or gynecologic staging course, does not teach procedure performance, and has not received formal clinician review. [1] [4]

sections.title: Worked modality decisions: keep observations and exclusions explicit
sections.narration: Use a second pass to test whether the report answers the requested question. There are four recurring mismatches. The referral may name a body region that the study did not cover. The requested comparison may require a feature that the two techniques do not depict in the same way. A protocol may be unknown even though a trial category is requested. Or the conclusion may be broader than the information in the image. The remedy is not to select a favored modality in every case. It is to identify which mismatch exists and explain it. The institutional examples on the Dana-Farber page are useful because they are concrete: it explicitly lists chest and abdomen body imaging; CT for initial staging and follow-up; advanced MRI examples including prostate, rectal, hepatobiliary, female pelvis and MR urography; and ultrasound assignments for abdominal, pelvic/genitourinary, thyroid, vascular and superficial soft-tissue examinations. The point is that the programme exposes learners to different questions and modalities, not that one modality should be used in all those clinical scenarios. [1] Fictional case one: a request asks for reassessment of a renal-region finding, but the only study provided is a limited ultrasound examination with no comparator. The ABR blueprint includes GU domains such as focal renal lesions and ultrasound, CT and MRI. That establishes what the parent board assesses, not a recommended test for this invented patient. A source-aware report should state the modality and what region is actually seen, identify any missing comparator and avoid claiming characterization beyond the available exam. The learner would ask the responsible clinician what specific question remains and consult the current local guideline or appropriate ACR scenario if a new study is being considered. [2] [3] Fictional case two: an initial abdominal CT is followed by an MRI that shows a small focus more clearly. It is not necessarily new disease. First check whether the focus was in the earlier scan's field and whether the earlier technique could show the feature now described. Then compare only the attribute that both studies represent reliably. A report can say “more conspicuous on the current technique” without converting that statement into “interval growth” or “new metastasis.” The distinction protects against comparing unlike observations. The ACR Appropriateness Criteria are scenario-specific references and the clinical question must be clear before a topic can guide modality selection. [3] Fictional case three: a pelvic follow-up includes an examination before and after surgery, with different coverage and sequences. The first pass should separate postoperative anatomy from a claim about cancer response. Identify which structures were imaged, whether the same region was included, and whether the report has access to pathology and the clinical timeline. The DFCI page includes pelvis and GU applications in its training description and says fellows interpret and protocol follow-up imaging, but it does not publish a complete postoperative decision tree. A course author should not fill that gap with invented institutional protocol. [1] Exercise: a report says “stable throughout the chest, abdomen and pelvis,” although only chest and upper abdomen are imaged. What is the best correction? Answer: narrow the conclusion to the imaged regions and state that the pelvis is not assessed in this examination. “Not included” is not equivalent to “normal.” If the clinical question requires pelvic assessment, the authorized team must decide whether the current study is adequate or another examination is appropriate. This is not a new imaging recommendation; it is a scope correction. [1] [3] An additional discipline is to preserve observation, inference and action as three separate statements. Observation: “the focus is more conspicuous on the current sequence.” Inference: “the appearance is indeterminate on this comparison.” Action: “provide prior images or obtain authorized review if a definitive comparison is clinically required.” The first is what the image shows; the second calibrates confidence; the third identifies a workflow need without ordering treatment. The ACR manual is a reference for contrast media issues, but it does not support creating an unsourced local reaction pathway. For any contrast concern, document the question and use the current manual and local policy through qualified staff. [4] Conclude the case by testing a statement against its evidence: Does the study actually include the relevant anatomy? Does the comparator allow change to be measured? Is the requested framework known? Does the sentence describe image evidence or a clinical decision? If one answer is no, narrow the claim or name the missing information. This modest method is transferable across CT, MRI and ultrasound while leaving actual protocols and patient care to the clinical service.
